abstract: Predictive fault management based on Artificial Intelligence (AI) can complement classical spacecraft Fault Detection, Isolation and Recovery (FDIR) by forecasting the current spacecraft behavior into the future and identifying deviations before hard limit violations occur. This paper presents the concept and modeling approaches of the AI4FDIR experiment, an onboard technology demonstrator implemented within the SeRANIS mission, which investigates multi-horizon time-series forecasting and anomaly detection under realistic operational constraints. The approach operates in three forecasting modes (short-, mid-, and long-term) that differ in lookback length, forecast horizon, and temporal resolution to cover both fast transient and slow drift anomalies. The experiment is designed for onboard inference on the mission’s AI-capable onboard computer (AI-OBC), enabling real-time predictive monitoring without interacting with the spacecraft’s nominal FDIR chain. The present pre-flight evaluation compares forecasting accuracy, anomaly-detection behavior, and development-workstation runtime/resource utilization to assess the suitability of the selected methods for future onboard predictive monitoring.

blocks.html: As spacecraft systems become more complex and operations increasingly rely on autonomy, fault management must provide not only safe reactions to failures but also early awareness of developing off-nominal behavior. Recent advances in AI enable data-driven models that learn expected telemetry dynamics and use predictions and forecasts to detect deviations from nominal behavior. Such predictive approaches are particularly relevant for subtle degradations and system-dependent effects that are difficult to capture with fixed thresholds. [1, 2]

Classical Fault Detection, Isolation and Recovery (FDIR) is typically rule-based, using limit checks, and predefined logic. While robust and flight-proven, these methods scale poorly with growing telemetry volume and may miss correlated effects across subsystems, or slowly evolving failure modes. Data-driven models can learn nominal temporal behavior directly from telemetry and provide forecasting-based consistency checks. Deviations between predicted and observed behavior can indicate anomalies earlier than threshold violations. [1, 2]

The Seamless Radio Access Network for Internet of Space (SeRANIS) mission provides an in-orbit testbed for advanced onboard processing and AI-based experiments. Its ATHENE-1 spacecraft is a ∼300 kg small-satellite and hosts more than 20 experimental payloads. The launch into a sun-synchronous Orbit at about 510 km altitude is expected for end of 2026. The AI4FDIR experiment is one of the payloads and investigates AI-based predictive fault management designed for onboard execution, enabling evaluation under realistic operational constraints and thereby increasing the technology readiness of AI-driven FDIR concepts. [2–4]

This paper presents the AI4FDIR experiment concept and its pre-flight evaluation for predictive fault management on ATHENE-1. The concept defines a deployable multihorizon forecasting pipeline with three operational modes and compares statistical, recurrent, convolutional, and detector-based methods under mode-dependent resampling. The results support model and mode selection for future in-orbit evaluation under onboard resource constraints. The remainder of the paper outlines the experiment setup and the onboard pipeline for time-series forecasting and anomaly detection, evaluates the selected models, and presents key results for multi-mode forecasting and anomaly detection. It concludes with a discussion of forecasting/runtime trade-offs, detector complementarity, and next steps toward onboard evaluation.
This section summarizes the AI4FDIR pre-flight evaluation, focusing on the trade-off between forecasting fidelity, anomaly-detection behavior, and runtime under the three mode definitions.

AI4FDIR is deployed as a non-interfering onboard technology demonstrator on ATHENE-1 as part of the SeRANIS mission. The experiment does not interface with, command, or modify the spacecraft’s nominal FDIR chain. Instead, it passively receives selected telemetry parameters and produces predictive outputs (multi-step forecasts) and anomaly detection results under realistic operational constraints.

The AI4FDIR experiment follows a streamlined on-board pipeline, see Figure 1. Selected telemetry is preprocessed (cleaning and scaling), then used to produce an in-sample prediction and an out-of-sample multi-step forecast. Anomaly detection is applied directly to the telemetry and to prediction/ forecast residuals, enabling both classical outlier detection and forecast-consistency checks against learned nominal dynamics.

Onboard Deployment and Constraints. All inference is intended for execution onboard the AI-OBC, which consists of an FPGA and two NVIDIA Jetson Xavier GPUequipped modules. Each Jetson Xavier provides a six-core NVIDIA Carmel Arm CPU, an NVIDIA Volta GPU with 48 Tensor Cores, and 16 GB RAM. The experiment design accounts for limited onboard computational resources and therefore trades temporal detail against computational load using mode-dependent resampling and model sizing. Since the AI-OBC engineering model was not available for the present evaluation, the runtime measurements as well as forecasting and anomaly-detection results were obtained on a development workstation equipped with an Intel Xeon CPU with 8 cores and 16 logical processors, an NVIDIA Quadro RTX 4000 GPU, and 64 GB RAM. The reported runtime and resource-utilization values in Section 2.3 are therefore used only for relative model comparison and do not represent AI-OBC execution margins.

Multi-horizon Forecasting Concept. To capture both rapid deviations and slow drifts in spacecraft telemetry, AI4FDIR operates in three forecasting modes (short-, mid-, and long-term). Each mode is defined by a specific combination of lookback length, forecast horizon, and sampling resolution. Resampling is applied to reduce the amount of data necessary for (re-)fitting the model and thus enable longer-range forecasting under limited onboard computational power. The mode definitions implemented in the current experiment setup are summarized in Table 1.

Dataset used for pre-flight validation. The telemetry used for evaluation is not ATHENE-1 flight telemetry, since SeRANIS has not yet entered operations. Instead, representative telemetry from the ESAIL mission, which is based on the same satellite platform as ATHENE-1, was used for pre-flight validation and model training. The dataset was provided by Spire Global, Inc. and covers 31 May 2021 to 1 June 2022. In-orbit evaluation on ATHENE-1 will extend the assessment to additional telemetry parameters and operational regimes.

blocks.html: Artificial Anomaly Injection. For systematic assessment beyond naturally occurring operational variations, the experiment supports injection of artificial anomalies (e.g., spikes, offsets, stuck-values, and drifts) to evaluate the sensitivity and robustness of forecasting- and detector-based anomaly identification under known conditions.

blocks.title: AI Models and Onboard Training Strategy

blocks.html: AI4FDIR implements multiple approaches for telemetry forecasting and anomaly detection to explore the trade space between model expressiveness, robustness, and on-board computational cost. The model hyperparameters and architectures used are summarized in Table 2.

Telemetry forecasting models. For forecasting, AI4FDIR considers one classical statistical baseline and several deep-learning sequence models. As statistical baseline, the Seasonal Auto-Regressive Integrated Moving Average (SARIMA) models the time series with AR/MA terms, differencing, and optional seasonal components and serves as an interpretable, low-cost baseline for near-linear and periodic telemetry. To capture non-linear and regime-dependent dynamics, Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) models learn temporal dependencies via gated recurrent states. This is a parameter- and mode-specific LSTM for fixed lookback, forecast, and resolution settings per mode with fixed model input and output shapes. Additionally, an Auto-Encoder (AE) style sequence-to-sequence (seq2seq) LSTM encodes a lookback window into a latent representation and decodes it into a coherent multi-step forecast trajectory. This LSTMseq2seq model maps variable-length lookback windows to multi-step forecasts, enabling more flexible horizon studies utilizing flexible model input and output shapes. Finally, a Temporal Convolutional Network (TCN) is included as a convolutional sequence model for efficient long-term forecasting using causal dilated convolutions, enabling parallel inference and offering attractive runtime properties for resource-constrained onboard deployment. [5–8]

blocks.html: Anomaly detection methods. To robustly detect different types of off-nominal behavior, AI4FDIR considers different detection strategies. Z-score thresholding flags samples whose standardized deviation from nominal statistics exceeds a threshold and provides a lightweight, explainable baseline for strong outliers. Local Outlier Factor (LOF) compares local neighborhood densities to identify context-dependent outliers, and a one-class Support Vector Machine (SVM) learns a boundary around nominal data in feature space to label novel patterns as anomalous. In addition, an LSTM-based autoencoder (LSTM-AE) is evaluated as a reconstruction-based detector trained on nominal lookback windows. A high reconstruction error is interpreted as anomalous behavior. [9–12] These detectors support both direct outlier detection and forecast-consistency checks.

Initialization and in-orbit adaptation strategy. Model initialization follows a staged approach aligned with operational constraints. The forecasting statistical models (SARIMA) and the light-weight detection models (SVM and LOF) are fitted directly onboard on the available onboard data, whereas the deep-learning models (LSTM, LSTMseq2seq, and TCN) are initialized from ground-trained weights and can be adapted in orbit using re-fitting on newly observed telemetry to account for distribution shifts (e.g., thermal environment, aging, or changes in operational regimes). Pre-trained mode- and parameter-specific models are used to avoid mixing incompatible time scales.

blocks.html: To assess the end-to-end pipeline, the evaluation in this paper focuses on the reaction-wheel-speed in x-direction (RWX) channel as a representative periodic telemetry parameter. Tables 3 and 4 summarize forecasting accuracy and runtime on the development workstation across all three modes, while Fig. 2 shows the long-term mode for visual comparison.

Across the long-term forecast horizon, SARIMA achieves the lowest forecast error for the periodic RWX case, while LSTM better preserves the evolving cycle qualitatively. LSTM-seq2seq shows the largest long-term forecast degradation, reflecting the sensitivity of the encoder-decoder configuration at inference time. TCN achieves the lowest mid-term forecast error and substantially lower longterm runtime than SARIMA, but its long-term accuracy remains below the SARIMA baseline for this periodic channel. These results indicate that model suitability depends on both telemetry dynamics and mode-specific resource constraints.

For detector evaluation, spike and offset anomalies were injected into the long-term RWX telemetry because the selected ESAIL subset did not contain labeled naturally occurring anomalies. Ground-truth labels are therefore defined exclusively by the known injection intervals. Figure 3 shows the injected signal and detector outputs, and Table 5 summarizes the resulting metrics.

Z-score detects the pronounced spike and sustained offset most reliably in this controlled univariate case, resulting in the highest recall among the evaluated detectors. SVM, LOF, and LSTM-AE mainly respond to locally unusual samples, such as the spike and the transition into or out of the offset interval, rather than continuously flagging the full shifted segment. SVM additionally raises false alarms at nominal regime changes, reflecting its sensitivity to the learned decision boundary. LOF emphasizes local density changes around the spike and offset transitions, while LSTM-AE produces no false positives but remains conservative under the selected reconstruction-error threshold.

blocks.html: AI4FDIR is implemented as a passive onboard experiment to evaluate predictive monitoring concepts under realistic mission constraints without coupling into the nominal FDIR chain. The RWX case study demonstrates the complete pre-flight pipeline, including multi-mode forecasting, runtime assessment on the development workstation, and controlled injected-anomaly detection.

Forecasting and runtime trade-offs. The results show that no single forecaster is optimal across all modes and constraints. SARIMA is highly competitive for strongly periodic telemetry and achieves the best long-term RWX forecast accuracy, but its long-term runtime is highest due to the fitting strategy. In contrast, the neural-network forecasters provide shorter forecasting cycles once initialized from pre-trained weights, with optional re-fitting where enabled. TCN illustrates this trade-off clearly, providing the lowest mid-term forecast error and the shortest long-term runtime, while not outperforming SARIMA in long-term forecast accuracy for the periodic RWX case. This motivates channel- and mode-dependent model selection rather than a single universal forecaster.

Multi-mode and detector strategy. The short-, mid-, and long-term modes separate anomaly time scales through different lookback lengths, forecast horizons, and resampling. This allows forecast reach and temporal resolution to be adapted to expected anomaly dynamics, detection latency, and available onboard resources. The injected spike and offset case further shows that detector behavior is complementary. Z-score is effective for large univariate deviations, SVM is sensitive to boundary changes, LOF emphasizes local inconsistency, and LSTM-AE behaves conservatively under the selected reconstruction-error threshold. Maintaining a small detector portfolio and tuning thresholds against mission-specific false-alarm budgets is therefore preferable to relying on a single scoring principle.

Outlook. Future work will extend the present univariate RWX evaluation toward multivariate and context-aware forecasting. The RW-speed telemetry channels will be evaluated jointly to capture coupled wheel behavior, and operational context features will be included to distinguish commanded mode changes from genuinely off-nominal behavior. Final runtime and memory profiling on the AI- OBC engineering model will be required to convert the measurements on the development workstation into on-board execution margins. XAI-based interpretation will be investigated as an additional step toward subsystem-level fault isolation and proactive mitigation.
